newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parties want EU envoys recalled from Iran.
newsitem.headline: German parties want EU envoys recalled from Iran.

text.p: Foreign policy experts from Germany's main political parties urged the European Union on Thursday to recall envoys from Iran after a Berlin court ruled Tehran ordered the 1992 killings of three Kurdish dissidents.

Karl Lamers, foreign policy spokesman for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, and Guenter Verheugen of the opposition Social Democrats said the envoys should be recalled while the EU considered the implications of Thursday's verdict.
"It is necessary to recall our ambassador and it would be good if our European partners did the same, to develop a joint European policy on Iran," Verheugen told German Radio.

Lamers said he agreed with Verheugen and said the EU policy of "critical dialogue" with Tehran should be suspended while the EU considered its options and also to await the results of next month's Iranian presidential elections.

"It (critical dialogue) must be suspended and reconsidered," Lamers said. "We must wait for the results of the elections in Iran. Before then there would be no success anyway in a continued dialogue."
But both Lamers and Verheugen stressed they were against isolating Iran completely.
"Breaking off diplomatic relations would be a serious mistake," Verheugen said. "But it would also be a serious mistake if we carried on as if nothing had happened."
The German Foreign Ministry declined any comment until after the court's opinion was read out in full.

Inside the Berlin courtroom, small groups of Iranian exiles burst into applause after hearing the court had sentenced the two main suspects in the case to life in jail. Two others were jailed, one for 11 years and the other for five years and three months.
Outside, over 1,000 Iranians crowded outside the Berlin court cheered, sang and danced when they heard the news.
Over 100 police were on hand to keep three Iranian exile groups -- Kurds, royalists and followers of the mujahideen resistance group --- away from each other.
A cheer went up from the crowd when an official of the National Council of Resistance of Iran read out a statement from the mujahideen leader Massoud Radjavi.
"For years, there has hardly been any doubt about the role of the criminal mullah regime's leadership in terrorist acts," he said.

"Now a European court has for the first time named (supreme religious leader Ayatollah Ali) Khamenei and (President Akbar Hashemi) Rafsanjani as the masterminds of the attack in Berlin and Tehran's state terrorism."

The court did not identify the Iranian leaders by name but said the attack could not have been carried out without orders from a committee for special operations. It specifically noted the president and religious leader were members.

A prominent Bonn politician, Free Democrat (FDP) deputy Juergen Moellemann, said Germany should now intensify the critical dialogue with Tehran rather than give it up as partners such as the United States have urged.
"A Berlin judge cannot decide how we organise our relations with countries around the world," he said. "If there are problems, one should actually intensify the dialogue."
Germany, Iran's biggest trading partner and most important friend in the West, said on Monday it might have to review relations after the verdict was known.
"The government is certain that it will not be taking part in this critical dialogue for the foreseeable future," the German Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

The policy of critical dialogue, championed by Germany, was initiated by the European Union back in 1992 in an effort to gain influence in Iran. Major allies, above all Britain and the United States, accuse Iran of state terrorism.
Iran has denied all responsibility for the murders and on Thursday the speaker of the Iranian parliament, Ali Akbar nateq-Nouri, dismissed the court verdict as "political".

The Foreign Ministry statement also said EU nations were considering joining Germany in recalling their ambassadors from Tehran in response to the Berlin court verdict. "The government regrets this development, especially since the Iranian and German peoples have enjoyed friendly relations for well over 100 years," the statement ended.
